content.body:
Frozen shoulder is a painful, progressive restriction of both active and passive glenohumeral movement, caused by inflammation and fibrosis of the joint capsule. That phrase — passive as well as active — is the whole diagnosis. It is what separates this condition from rotator cuff related shoulder pain, where passive range is preserved.

There is no laboratory test and no imaging finding that makes the diagnosis. It is clinical.

content.text: Both of its names are wrong

rows: Descriptive rather than mechanistic — but harmless, and patients understand it
There are no adhesions, and the process is not primarily an "-itis". Both halves of the word are inaccurate

content.body: The capsule does not stick to itself — it contracts and thickens. "Adhesive capsulitis" survives mostly in coding systems and textbook titles. Frozen shoulder is the better clinical term, and the one to use with patients.

• Primary (idiopathic) — no identifiable cause. The classic presentation, typically between 40 and 60.
  • Secondary — occurring alongside a recognised association. Conventionally split into systemic (diabetes, thyroid disease), extrinsic (stroke, cardiac or thoracic surgery, prolonged immobilisation) and intrinsic (rotator cuff pathology, after shoulder surgery or trauma).

The distinction matters less for treatment than for expectation: secondary frozen shoulder — particularly in diabetes — tends to be more resistant and slower to settle.

content.label: Definition
content.text: Painful restriction of passive glenohumeral movement, with external rotation affected first and worst, in a shoulder whose radiographs show no structural explanation.

content.body: If passive external rotation is preserved, it is not frozen shoulder. If the radiograph shows advanced glenohumeral osteoarthritis or a locked posterior dislocation, the restriction has another cause.

Frozen shoulder affects roughly 2–5% of the general population, and 13–30% of people with diabetes. Estimates vary — some reviews put the general-population figure below 2% — because case definitions differ and there is no diagnostic test to anchor them.

  • Age 40–60 is the typical window. A frozen shoulder outside it should prompt a second look at the diagnosis.
  • Women are affected somewhat more often than men.
  • The non-dominant arm is involved slightly more often.
  • A substantial minority go on to develop it in the other shoulder, usually not simultaneously. Recurrence in the same shoulder is uncommon.

content.text: Diabetes is the association that matters

content.body: A 2026 meta-analysis of 10 studies and 351,486 participants found a pooled odds ratio of 3.69 (95% CI 2.99–4.56) for the association between diabetes and frozen shoulder.

rows: Pooled prevalence of frozen shoulder in diabetes
Pooled odds ratio, diabetes vs no diabetes

content.body: Type 1 diabetes carries the stronger association, and Mendelian randomisation work suggests the link there may be causal. In type 2, the association appears more mediated by metabolic and vascular factors. The authors caution that unmeasured confounding may inflate these estimates.

rows: Dupuytren's disease — a shared fibroproliferative tendency
Cardiac and thoracic surgery · stroke · breast cancer surgery and radiotherapy · shoulder trauma or surgery · any prolonged immobilisation
Rotator cuff disease, particularly where pain has led to disuse

content.body:
Check HbA1c and thyroid function in anyone presenting with a frozen shoulder, unless recently done. The association with diabetes is strong enough that frozen shoulder can be the presentation that uncovers it — and knowing the glycaemic status changes the prognosis you give, since diabetic frozen shoulder is typically more stubborn and slower to resolve.

Avoid prolonged immobilisation after any shoulder injury or surgery, particularly in a patient with diabetes. This is the one risk factor that is squarely within your control.

content.label: Source
content.text: Source: Hernigou P, Scarlat MM. The diabetic shoulder: association between diabetes mellitus and adhesive capsulitis — a systematic review and meta-analysis. International Orthopaedics 2026;50:839–851.

content.body: One structure explains most of what you find on examination: the coracohumeral ligament, and the rotator interval it spans. Understanding why makes the examination findings predictable rather than something to memorise.

The glenohumeral joint has the largest range of any joint in the body, and it achieves that partly because its capsule is redundant. The slack hangs inferiorly as the axillary recess — a fold that unfurls as the arm elevates. A normal glenohumeral joint accommodates roughly 10–15 mL of fluid.

In frozen shoulder that capacity falls, often below 10 mL. The capsule has not stuck to anything; it has thickened and contracted, and the slack that permitted movement is gone.

A triangular gap in the capsule between subscapularis below and supraspinatus above, with the coracoid base at its medial apex. It contains:

  • The coracohumeral ligament — from the base of the coracoid to both tuberosities
  • The superior glenohumeral ligament
  • The long head of biceps, passing through on its way to the groove

This is the region most consistently abnormal in frozen shoulder. Arthroscopy and MRI show a thickened, contracted coracohumeral ligament and an obliterated rotator interval, often before anything else is apparent.
Each capsular structure restrains a different movement, and the one that fails first determines the pattern you see.

rows: External rotation with the arm at the side
The earliest and most severe loss — the hallmark finding
Limits rotation as the arm comes up
Inferior glenohumeral ligament complex and axillary recess
Loss of abduction and overhead reach

content.body: So the sequence is not arbitrary. The structure that tightens first is the one that restrains external rotation in adduction — which is exactly the movement you test with the elbow at the patient's side, and exactly the movement they cannot do.

content.text: A note on the capsular pattern

content.body:
Classic teaching holds that the capsule restricts movement in a fixed proportional order: external rotation worst, then abduction, then internal rotation. It is a useful heuristic and it fits most patients.

It is not, however, a validated rule. The evidence that the ratio holds consistently across patients is weak. Treat it as a pattern to expect, not a criterion that must be satisfied — and remember that loss of passive external rotation is the finding that matters, not the proportions between movements.
Two processes run in the capsule: inflammation and fibrosis. They overlap rather than following one another neatly, which is why the tidy three-stage model described later is a simplification.

content.text: The capsule behaves like Dupuytren's disease

content.body:
The histology is the most useful thing to know. Capsular fibroblasts proliferate and differentiate into myofibroblasts — contractile cells that lay down dense type I and III collagen and actively pull the tissue tighter. The appearance closely resembles Dupuytren's disease, and the two conditions share genetic associations and signalling pathways.

That is why patients with Dupuytren's are over-represented, and why the capsule does not merely stiffen but actively shortens.

rows: Synovitis and inflammatory mediator release. NF-κB and leptin/JAK–STAT signalling dominate. Alarmins such as HMGB1 amplify the response
Inflammatory signalling stimulates fibroblasts to secrete TGF-β1 — the central fibrotic driver
TGF-β/Smad signalling drives extracellular matrix synthesis, fibroblast proliferation and myofibroblast differentiation. Wnt/β-catenin and other pathways reinforce it
An imbalance between matrix metalloproteinases and their inhibitors (TIMPs) means matrix is deposited faster than it is broken down

content.body:
Oxidative stress sustains the loop: raised NOX4 and reduced superoxide dismutase increase reactive oxygen species, which further activate TGF-β.

Immune cells are involved throughout — Th17 cells producing IL-17A, and macrophages whose failure to switch from a pro-inflammatory to a resolving phenotype may be why the process does not simply settle.

This is the most satisfying mechanism in the condition. Advanced glycation end products accumulate in long-lived collagen and act through the RAGE receptor to promote inflammation and fibrosis. Glycation also cross-links collagen directly, stiffening it independently of any cellular process. Leptin signalling provides a second route in metabolic disease.

So the diabetic capsule is both more likely to start down this path and more resistant to coming back from it — which matches what you see clinically.

Frozen shoulder is disproportionately painful for a condition with no fracture, no tear and no infection. The explanation is new blood vessels and new nerve fibres growing into the capsule, alongside active synovitis. Pain is produced by an inflamed, newly innervated tissue — not by the stiffness.

That has a direct clinical consequence: the pain and the stiffness are different problems with different treatments. Anti-inflammatory measures address the first and do little for the second.

• What triggers it. No upstream initiating event has been identified in primary disease.
  • Why the shoulder. The capsule elsewhere does not behave this way.
  • Why it affects some diabetics and not others — how systemic factors lower the threshold in local capsular fibroblasts is unresolved.
  • Whether the pathways can be targeted. TGF-β inhibition is attractive in theory; no human data support it in this condition.

content.label: Source
content.text: Source: Guo T, Hua Y, Liu X, et al. Signaling pathway networks in frozen shoulder fibrosis: from inflammatory initiation to fibrotic progression. Frontiers in Medicine 2026;13.
Natural history — and why the classic account does not hold

content.body: The single most repeated statement about frozen shoulder — that it is self-limiting and resolves completely within one to three years — is not supported by the evidence. This matters, because it is also the statement most often used to justify doing nothing.
Wong and colleagues searched for studies with untreated or no-treatment comparison groups and at least six months of follow-up. From 508 citations they found seven that qualified.

rows: Untreated patients regained some range of motion, but not full recovery, at 1–4 years
Most improvement occurred early, not late — which contradicts the phased recovery model

content.body: Their conclusion is unusually blunt for a systematic review:

content.label: Quote
content.text: "The theory of recovery phases leading to complete resolution without treatment for frozen shoulder is unfounded."

content.body: Separately, one case series found 41% still symptomatic at a mean of 4.4 years (range 2–20).

Do not promise spontaneous resolution. It is a promise you cannot keep, and when the shoulder is still stiff at eighteen months the patient will remember that you made it.

The "thawing comes last" model is probably backwards. If most improvement happens early, then waiting for a late thawing phase means waiting for something that may not arrive.

Watchful waiting is harder to defend than it looks. The rationale for leaving a frozen shoulder alone rested on a natural history that the evidence does not support.

Some residual restriction is common — and frequently not disabling. Many patients end up with a measurable deficit, particularly in external rotation, that does not limit what they actually do.

The evidence here is low quality in both directions. These are small studies, inconsistently defined, with untreated groups that were rarely untreated by design.

So the accurate statement is not "frozen shoulder does not resolve." It is: we do not reliably know what untreated frozen shoulder does, and the confident claim of complete spontaneous recovery has never been demonstrated. Say that, rather than either version of the certainty.

content.label: Source
content.text: Source: Wong CK, Levine WN, Deo K, et al. Natural history of frozen shoulder: fact or fiction? A systematic review. Physiotherapy 2017;103(1):40–47.
The staging model — how to use it, and where it fails

content.body: The classical model divides the condition into three stages. Know it, because the literature and your colleagues are written in it. Do not plan treatment from it.

rows: Pain, increasing. Night pain prominent. Range progressively lost
Stiffness. Pain eases but range is at its worst. Function is most limited

content.body:
The durations are unreliable. The quoted ranges overlap so widely that they predict nothing for an individual patient. A total of 2–42 months is not a prognosis.

The stages blur. Patients do not step from one to the next. Inflammation and fibrosis run concurrently in the capsule, and the clinical picture reflects that.

The sequence may be wrong. The model implies recovery comes late. The best available longitudinal data show most improvement happens early, which is the opposite.

It invites waiting. The practical effect of a three-stage model ending in spontaneous thawing is to make doing nothing look like a plan.
Forget the month count. Ask one question at every visit:

content.label: Key Takeaway
content.text: Is this shoulder dominated by pain, or by stiffness?

content.body: That is the only staging that changes what you do.

rows: Night pain, pain at rest, pain before end range
Pain mainly at end range, sleeping better, function limited by reach
Settle the pain — intra-articular corticosteroid, analgesia, sleep, gentle movement within comfort
Restore range — sustained stretching, mobilisation, progressive loading
Aggressive stretching — provokes, and achieves nothing while the capsule is inflamed
Waiting — the inflammation has gone; only mechanical input will change the range

content.body: A patient can move back and forth between these. Reassess each visit rather than assuming they have progressed.

content.label: Key Takeaway
content.text: The practical rule: stretch hard into a painful, inflamed shoulder and you will make it worse. Wait patiently beside a stiff, settled shoulder and you will waste months. Matching the treatment to which of the two you are looking at is most of the skill in managing this condition.

content.body: The diagnosis is usually made from the history before you touch the patient. A middle-aged person describes shoulder pain that came on without real injury, got worse over weeks, and has now been joined by a stiffness that is becoming the bigger problem.

• Insidious onset, with no trauma or only a trivial incident that the patient has over-interpreted
  • Pain builds over weeks to months, then range begins to go
  • Night pain is prominent — often the presenting complaint, and often severe. They cannot lie on that side
  • Pain is deep and diffuse, frequently referred to the deltoid insertion, and hard for the patient to localise with one finger
  • Sharp, catching pain on sudden unguarded movement — reaching to stop a door, grabbing a rail. This is characteristic
  • They are protecting the arm, holding it in adduction and internal rotation

content.text: The functional losses that give it away

content.body: Patients rarely say "I've lost external rotation." They say:

rows: "I can't reach my back pocket / do my bra up / tuck my shirt in"
"I can't reach for my seatbelt" / "turning the wheel hurts"
"I can't wash or dry my hair"
"I can't reach the shelf / hang the washing"
Night pain — and a marker of how irritable it is

content.body:
The associations, because they change your expectations and your workup:

  • Diabetes — diagnosed or suspected. Ask about thirst, weight change, family history if undiagnosed
  • Thyroid disease
  • Dupuytren's disease — ask them to show you their palms
  • Recent immobilisation, shoulder surgery or trauma
  • Cardiac or thoracic surgery, stroke, breast cancer treatment
  • A previous frozen shoulder on the other side

The trajectory, because it tells you which problem you are treating:

  • Is the pain getting worse, stable, or settling?
  • Is the stiffness getting worse, stable, or improving?
  • How long since it started?
  • How badly is it disturbing sleep?

A shoulder with worsening pain and increasing restriction is behaving differently from one where pain has settled and only the stiffness remains — and they need different treatment.

• Significant trauma preceding onset — think fracture, dislocation, acute cuff tear
  • Onset outside 40–60, particularly in a young patient
  • Systemic features — fever, weight loss, night sweats, known malignancy
  • Neurological symptoms, or weakness disproportionate to pain
  • A history of seizure, electrocution or high-energy trauma — locked posterior dislocation presents with exactly this pattern of restriction and is classically missed
One finding makes the diagnosis: loss of passive external rotation with the elbow at the patient's side. Everything else is confirmation or exclusion.

Patient seated or supine, elbow tucked against the trunk and flexed to 90°, forearm neutral. Passively rotate the forearm outward. Hold the elbow against the body — patients abduct to cheat.

  • In frozen shoulder, this is restricted and painful, with a firm, abrupt, capsular end feel
  • In rotator cuff related shoulder pain, it is free

If passive external rotation is full, look for another diagnosis.

This is the structural signature of the condition. In a cuff problem, the patient cannot lift the arm but you can lift it for them. In frozen shoulder you cannot either — active and passive range are restricted to roughly the same degree, because the block is mechanical rather than painful inhibition.
Use an inclinometer, goniometer or smartphone application — not visual estimation. These numbers are your outcome measure, and you will be comparing them in six weeks.

rows: The key measure. Lost first and worst
Only if they can get there
The functional loss patients complain about most

content.body: Always compare with the other side, and record both. A "restriction" means nothing without the contralateral number.

The commonest measurement error. A stiff glenohumeral joint recruits the scapulothoracic joint, and the patient produces apparently reasonable elevation by shrugging and tilting the scapula. Place a hand on the scapula, or watch from behind, and you will see the true glenohumeral range is far less than the arm position suggests.

The visible compensation — the shrug sign — is itself a useful observation.
Strength is usually preserved when tested within the available range, though testing may hurt. Marked weakness, particularly out of proportion to pain, points away from this diagnosis.

content.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content.text: Do not try to interpret rotator cuff special tests in a stiff shoulder. Hawkins-Kennedy, Neer, the empty and full can — all of them are positive when the capsule is tight and everything hurts at end range. They tell you nothing here. This is a common source of a wrong second diagnosis.

content.body:
• Cervical spine screen — referred pain is in the differential
  • Inspect for wasting — disuse wasting of deltoid and the cuff is common and does not imply nerve injury
  • Check the palms for Dupuytren's nodules
  • Palpation is largely unhelpful — tenderness is diffuse

There is no validated cut-off. Commonly used working definitions require passive external rotation reduced to less than 50% of the opposite side, or restriction in at least two planes, together with normal radiographs.

Treat these as conventions, not criteria. The diagnosis rests on the pattern: a painful shoulder, insidious onset, passive restriction with external rotation worst, and a radiograph that shows nothing to explain it.

The differential splits cleanly on two questions, and asking them in order resolves almost every case.

  1. Is passive external rotation restricted? If no — it is not frozen shoulder. Look at the cuff.
  2. If yes, does the radiograph explain it? If yes — it is osteoarthritis or a locked posterior dislocation, not frozen shoulder.

That is why the radiograph matters here and barely matters in rotator cuff disease: two conditions produce an identical examination finding, and only imaging separates them.

content.text: The conditions that restrict passive external rotation

rows: Older patient, crepitus, gradual. Radiograph: joint space loss, osteophytes, inferior humeral head osteophyte

History of seizure, electrocution or significant trauma. External rotation often blocked at or before neutral. Axillary or modified axial view is essential — the AP can look deceptively normal. Classically missed for months
Acute, systemic upset, fever, exquisite pain on any movement. A surgical emergency
Other joints, morning stiffness, raised inflammatory markers
The history gives it. Managed similarly, but prognosis differs

content.text: The conditions that do not restrict passive external rotation

rows: Passive range preserved. Painful arc, pain on resisted testing
Weakness out of proportion to pain, positive lag signs, passive range preserved
Severe, abrupt, out-of-keeping pain. Guarding may mimic stiffness. Radiograph shows the deposit
Neck movements reproduce it, dermatomal distribution, neurological signs
Over 50, bilateral shoulder and pelvic girdle, marked morning stiffness, raised ESR/CRP
Severe pain for days, then profound weakness and wasting as pain settles
Night pain unrelieved by position, systemic features, known primary. Pancoast tumour can present as shoulder pain
Steroid use, sickle cell, alcohol excess, previous fracture
Often post-stroke or post-fracture. Allodynia, swelling, trophic and vasomotor change

content.body:
Locked posterior dislocation. It restricts external rotation, has a normal-looking AP radiograph, and gets labelled frozen shoulder. If external rotation is blocked at or before neutral — particularly after a seizure or electrocution — get an axillary view before you accept the diagnosis.

Polymyalgia rheumatica. Bilateral shoulder girdle pain and stiffness in an older patient is PMR until proven otherwise. A bilateral simultaneous frozen shoulder is uncommon; PMR is not.

content.label: Key Takeaway
content.text: A frozen shoulder that is not improving at all is a diagnosis worth revisiting, not just a treatment to escalate.

content.body: The diagnosis is clinical. Imaging exists to exclude, not to confirm. No imaging finding is required, and none is sufficient.

content.text: Radiographs — the one study everyone should have

content.body:
True AP (Grashey) and an axillary or modified axial view.

In frozen shoulder the radiograph is normal, or shows only disuse osteopenia. Its job is to exclude the two conditions that produce the same restriction:

  • Glenohumeral osteoarthritis — joint space loss, osteophytes
  • Locked posterior dislocation — and this is why the axillary view is not optional. The AP can look near-normal, and this diagnosis is routinely missed for months

It will also show a calcific deposit, a fracture, or a bone lesion.

Not necessary for diagnosis, but useful in two situations: excluding rotator cuff pathology when the picture is mixed, and guiding injection.

If performed, supportive findings include thickening of the axillary pouch capsule (a 4 mm cut-off gave 94% sensitivity and 98% specificity in one study), coracohumeral ligament thickening (no agreed cut-off — compare both sides), rotator interval hypervascularity, and restricted gliding of supraspinatus. A meta-analysis of combined ultrasound criteria reported 88% sensitivity and 96% specificity.

Not required. Reserve it for genuine diagnostic doubt, or when another pathology needs excluding.

If it is done, the findings that support the diagnosis:

rows: T2 hyperintensity in the axillary pouch / inferior glenohumeral ligament
Obliteration of the subcoracoid fat triangle

content.body:
Note the pattern: the specific findings are not sensitive. A normal-looking MRI does not exclude frozen shoulder, which is another reason not to order one to make the diagnosis.

MR arthrography and contrast-enhanced MRI are not justified for suspected frozen shoulder.

rows: Strong association; may be the presentation that uncovers diabetes; changes the prognosis you give
If bilateral, systemic features, or over 50 with girdle symptoms

content.label: Key Takeaway
content.text:
Radiograph for everyone. Bloods for everyone. Ultrasound or MRI only when the diagnosis is in doubt or another condition needs excluding.
If you find yourself ordering an MRI to confirm a frozen shoulder, re-examine instead — the answer is in the passive external rotation.

content.label: Source
content.text: Source: Adhesive Capsulitis of the Shoulder: Current Concepts on the Diagnostic Work-Up and Evidence-Based Protocol for Radiological Evaluation.

content.body: Treat the pain early and decisively; treat the stiffness mechanically and patiently; and do not do either at the wrong time. That is the whole strategy.

1 · Pain and stiffness are different problems. Pain comes from synovitis and neoinnervation; stiffness comes from a contracted capsule. Corticosteroid treats the first and does little for the second. Stretching treats the second and inflames the first. Matching intervention to problem is most of the skill.

2 · Early is better. The benefit of intra-articular corticosteroid is greatest in shoulders of less than one year's duration. Waiting to see whether it settles spends the window in which the best-supported treatment works.

3 · Be honest about what treatment achieves. No intervention has been shown to shorten the overall course of the disease. What good treatment does is reduce the pain and improve the function along the way — which is worth a great deal, but is a different claim from curing it.
The largest synthesis — 65 randomised trials, 4,097 participants — reached an unusually actionable conclusion.

rows: Intra-articular corticosteroid vs placebo or no treatment
Pain improved by about 1.4 points on a 10-point scale early, 1.0 late; external rotation gained 5–7°; function improved. Benefit persisted to about 6 months
Favoured injection for pain and early function
External rotation gained a further 11.6° in the early short term
Statistically better pain, but the authors judged the difference clinically insignificant

content.label: Evidence note
content.text: The authors' recommendation: intra-articular corticosteroid "should be offered to patients with frozen shoulder at first contact," combined with a home exercise programme.

content.body: The caveats are real. Certainty of evidence was mostly moderate to low, many differences fell below the minimal clinically important threshold, and trial sequential analysis did not confirm the advantage of injection over physiotherapy for pain.

content.text: The treatment pathway in one sentence

content.label: Key Takeaway
content.text: Injection plus a home exercise programme at first contact; escalate to distension or a procedure only if that has genuinely failed.
What to tell the patient from the outset

content.body:
• This is a painful condition that takes many months, and nothing available will make it quick
  • The pain usually settles before the stiffness does
  • We treat the pain now so that you can sleep and move; we work on the range as the pain allows
  • Some stiffness may persist — and most people function well despite it
  • Do not stop moving the arm. Immobilisation makes this worse, and may be how it started

content.label: Source
content.text: Source: Challoumas D, Biddle M, McLean M, Millar NL. Comparison of Treatments for Frozen Shoulder: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA Netw Open 2020;3(12):e2029581.

content.body: This is the single best-supported treatment, and it should be offered early rather than held in reserve. It treats the synovitis that produces the pain. It does not dissolve the fibrosis that produces the stiffness.

content.text: Timing — the decision that matters most

content.body:
Offer it at first contact, particularly when the shoulder has been symptomatic for less than one year. The benefit is greatest early and diminishes as the condition becomes stiffness-dominated.

The common error is to try exercise alone for three months first. That spends the window in which the injection works best, in a patient who is not sleeping.

Intra-articular (glenohumeral) is the target. Compared with subacromial injection it gave slightly better early pain (about 0.6 points) and late function, with no difference by mid-term.

That difference is small. If the glenohumeral joint is difficult to access, a subacromial injection is a reasonable alternative — and it may cause less glycaemic disturbance in diabetic patients.

Use ultrasound guidance where available. Blind glenohumeral injection is substantially less accurate than blind subacromial injection, and in a joint whose capsule is contracted and whose volume is reduced, accuracy matters.

There is no established optimal dose. Common practice is 20–40 mg of triamcinolone or equivalent, with local anaesthetic.

On number: start with one and reassess. A partial response may justify a second. Repeated injections are not supported — if two have not produced meaningful benefit, the problem is not one that more steroid will solve, and it is time to reconsider the diagnosis or escalate.
This is not optional, and the numbers make the case:

rows: +11.6° external rotation in the early short term
Pain improved by 0.5 points — small, but real

content.body: The injection opens a window of reduced pain. The exercise is what turns that window into range. An injection given without a programme attached wastes most of its value.

content.text: Diabetes — what to warn them about

content.body: Blood glucose rises transiently after injection, and the rise is larger the worse the control.

Glucose returned to baseline by day 2.

So: warn every diabetic patient, advise closer monitoring on the first day, and be more cautious the higher the HbA1c. This is a reason to monitor, not a reason to withhold.
Post-injection flare, skin atrophy and depigmentation at the needle site, facial flushing, and — rarely — infection. All uncommon, and all worth mentioning briefly when consenting.

content.label: Key Takeaway
content.text: The prescription, in one line: intra-articular corticosteroid under ultrasound guidance at first contact, plus a home exercise programme starting the same week, with glucose monitoring advice if diabetic.

content.body: The intensity must match the irritability. This is the opposite of the instinct, which is that a stiff shoulder needs to be stretched hard. Stretch hard into an inflamed capsule and you will make it worse and slower.

content.text: The evidence that should change your instinct

content.body: Diercks and Stevens followed 77 patients with idiopathic frozen shoulder for two years, comparing intensive passive stretching and manual mobilisation against "supervised neglect" — reassurance, exercises kept within pain limits, and encouragement to use the arm normally.

columns: Normal or near-normal painless function at 2 years

content.body: The study was prospective but its randomisation is not clearly described, so treat the size of the difference cautiously. The direction, however, is consistent with the pathophysiology: forcing an inflamed, actively fibrosing capsule provokes it.
Goal: keep what range there is, settle the pain, protect sleep. Not gain range.

rows: Trunk bent forward, arm hanging relaxed, movement driven by trunk sway
The shoulder is a passenger. No cuff or deltoid contraction is required, and the arm's own weight gives gentle distraction. Almost nothing is asked of an irritable joint
Lying down, stick or good hand lifting the arm

Supine inverts where gravity bites. Standing, the load rises as the arm elevates; lying down the arm starts supported and moves toward vertical, where the moment arm falls to zero. You get access to elevation at a fraction of the muscular cost
Hand on a towel, lean the body in
The surface carries part of the limb's weight, and the patient grades their own dose by how far they lean. Self-limiting, which matters in someone frightened of the movement
Shrug, retract, protract; thoracic extension over a chair back; side-lying open-book
Range that does not come from the glenohumeral joint. It preserves total arm elevation and stops the whole girdle stiffening alongside the capsule
Everything it can still do, deliberately
Prevents learned non-use — and immobilisation is a risk factor for this condition, so protecting the arm completely risks making it worse

content.body: Do not stretch to end range, apply end-range mobilisation, or push through pain at this stage.

Once the pain has settled and the limit is mechanical, the approach reverses.

Low load, long duration. Collagenous tissue lengthens through creep, which responds to sustained gentle tension, not brief forceful pulls. A 30–60 second hold at the end of comfortable range, repeated, does more than a hard two-second stretch — and provokes far less.

Little and often. Three to five short sessions daily beats one long one. The capsule needs frequent exposure, and short sessions are what patients actually do.

Four directions, each taken to the point of stretch but not pain:

rows: Elbow pinned at the side, stick or doorframe pushing the forearm outward
The structure that contracts first and worst. The highest-yield stretch in the condition — and the one patients most often perform wrong by letting the elbow drift into abduction
Supine assisted with a stick; wall or table slides
Restores overhead reach. Supine first, standing later
Hand behind the back, towel assisted from above
Posterior capsule and posterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament
The loss patients complain about most — fastening a bra, a back pocket, tucking a shirt in
Opposite hand drawing the arm across the chest
Reaching across the body: seatbelt, opposite shoulder, washing the other arm
Supine, elbow supported on the bed
Anterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament
Add only once elevation allows it. This is the position overhead function actually needs, and a shoulder stretched only at the side is not prepared for it

content.body:
Technique points that decide whether the stretch works

  • Pin the elbow for external rotation. Without a towel between elbow and ribs, patients abduct and stretch nothing
  • Stabilise the scapula for elevation, or they shrug and the glenohumeral joint never moves
  • Hold, don't bounce. Bouncing is brief high force — exactly the stimulus that provokes rather than lengthens
  • Breathe through it. Breath-holding means the effort is too high

content.text: Strengthening — and why it is not optional

content.body:
Months of guarding weakens the deltoid and the cuff, and a shoulder that regains range without strength is not recovered: the arm feels heavy, unreliable and tires quickly, and patients describe this as still being unwell even when the goniometer says otherwise.

There is a second reason. Over months of restriction the patient has built substitution patterns — shrugging, trunk leaning, scapular hitching. Range alone does not undo them. Loading the shoulder through its restored range is what retrains the movement.

Sequence:

  1. Isometrics first — no range is travelled, so they are tolerable early. External rotation at the side is the priority, mirroring the stretch
  2. Isotonic loading through the available range as pain allows — external rotation, scaption, rows
  3. Progress by load, through whatever range exists, rather than waiting for full range before starting

content.text: The dosing rule to give the patient

content.label: Key Takeaway
content.text:
You should feel a stretch, not a sharp pain. It should ease within a few minutes of stopping. And it must not wake you more that night.
If it hurts for an hour afterwards, or disturbs your sleep, that was too much — do less tomorrow, not more.

content.body:
Trials comparing supervised physiotherapy with a well-taught home programme have not shown a consistent advantage for supervision. Given that this runs for months, a home programme the patient will actually do is worth more than clinic sessions they attend for six weeks and then stop.

Use supervised sessions to teach the technique, check it, and progress it — not to deliver the treatment.
Adherence, over months. Which means: few exercises, clear rules, a reason they understand, and a review that looks at the numbers rather than asking how they feel.

content.label: Source
content.text: Source: Diercks RL, Stevens M. Gentle thawing of the frozen shoulder: supervised neglect versus intensive physical therapy in 77 patients, followed for two years. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2004;13:499–502.

content.body: The largest trial ever conducted in this condition found that none of these is clearly better than structured physiotherapy with an injection. That should shape how readily you escalate.

After a genuine trial of corticosteroid injection plus a home exercise programme — in practice around three to six months — in a patient whose stiffness is still materially limiting them.

"Genuine" is doing work in that sentence. A patient who had one injection and two physiotherapy appointments has not failed conservative treatment.
503 adults with primary frozen shoulder, randomised across 35 UK hospitals to three arms, with the Oxford Shoulder Score at 12 months as the primary outcome.

rows: Steroid injection, then mobilisation and a graduated home programme — up to 12 sessions over 12 weeks
Capsule stretched and torn under GA, with steroid injection, then physiotherapy
Anterior capsule divided arthroscopically, then manipulation ± steroid, then physiotherapy

content.body:
All differences fell below the pre-specified 4–5 point threshold for clinical importance. ACR beat ESP by 3.06 points and MUA by 2.01 — statistically significant, clinically not.

Four further findings matter more than the headline:

  • At 3 months ACR was doing worse than the other two — the surgical recovery costs you a quarter of a year
  • Serious adverse events: ACR 8 (4%), MUA 2 (1%), ESP none
  • Cost-effectiveness: MUA had about an 86% probability of being cost-effective at £20,000/QALY; ESP about 14%; ACR essentially zero
  • ESP patients more often needed further treatment; ACR patients needed the fewest

content.label: Evidence note
content.text: The authors' conclusion: all three produce substantial improvement, none is clearly superior, and arthroscopic capsular release should be used more selectively — when less invasive options have failed.

rows: Fluid injected under pressure to distend and tear the capsule — steroid, local anaesthetic and saline, volumes 9–100 mL
Capsule torn by controlled passive force under anaesthesia, with steroid
Capsule divided under direct vision, then manipulated
Ranked highest for late short-term pain in network analysis, but the advantage over injection alone was judged clinically insignificant
No worse than ACR at 12 months; most cost-effective option
Marginally highest score at 12 months; worse at 3 months; highest complication rate
Humeral or glenoid fracture, soft tissue injury, brachial plexus injury — overall complication rate around 0.4%
Axillary nerve injury — stay at least 1 cm from the glenoid rim; infection; highest serious adverse event rate
A reasonable step up from injection alone, with modest expectations
The default escalation when conservative treatment has genuinely failed

content.body:
Hydrodilatation. The optimal volume and mixture are unknown. Expect a transient gain in range and disability rather than a transformation; the long-term effect on external rotation is unclear.

Manipulation. The most cost-effective escalation, and the one the trial data support as a default. It is not risk-free — fracture is the complication that matters, and the risk is higher in osteoporotic bone.

Capsular release. Reserve it. Less extensive releases appear to give better function and pain than more extensive ones, with no difference in complications. Routine subscapularis release is controversial.

All three need a physiotherapy programme afterwards. The procedure creates range; without immediate and sustained exercise, the capsule re-contracts and you have spent a general anaesthetic for nothing.

content.label: Source
content.text: Source: Rangan A, Brealey SD, Keding A, et al. Management of adults with primary frozen shoulder in secondary care (UK FROST): a multicentre, pragmatic, three-arm, superiority randomised clinical trial. Lancet 2020;396:977–89.

content.body: The two decision points are the whole pathway: has the pain settled decides whether you are allowed to work on range, and is it improving by three to six months decides whether to escalate. Everything else follows.

Mrs. R.K., 54. Right shoulder, 4 months. Type 2 diabetes, HbA1c 7.8%.

Insidious onset, no injury. Night pain waking her 3–4 times, cannot lie on the right side. Cannot fasten her bra or reach the seatbelt.

Examination: passive external rotation 10° right, 65° left. Passive elevation 95° right, 170° left. Hand behind back to buttock only. Firm capsular end feel. Strength preserved. Radiograph including axillary view: normal.

Assessment: primary frozen shoulder, right. Pain-predominant.

rows: Ultrasound-guided intra-articular corticosteroid, 40 mg triamcinolone with local anaesthetic. Warn about glucose — expect a rise of around 5 mmol/L (90 mg/dL) for about 24 hours given her HbA1c; monitor closely on day 1
HbA1c and thyroid function. Education: the five messages, especially stretch not pain
Pendulums; supine assisted elevation with a stick; assisted external rotation at the side. 10 repetitions, 4–5 times daily, within comfort. Keep using the arm for everything it can do
Off the right side; small pillow supporting the right elbow when supine
A stretch, not a sharp pain. Eases within minutes. Must not increase night pain
4 weeks — remeasure passive ER, elevation and hand-behind-back

content.body:
At review, if pain has settled: progress to the stiffness programme — sustained 30–60 second holds at end of comfortable range, four directions, three to five times daily. Begin isometric strengthening.

At review, if pain has not settled: reconsider the diagnosis, and consider a second injection. Do not start aggressive stretching.

At 3–6 months, if function remains materially limited despite adherence: refer for manipulation under anaesthesia. Expect her diabetes to make this slower throughout.

Passive external rotation, passive elevation, hand-behind-back level — both sides, with an inclinometer. These three numbers are the whole outcome measure, and without them you cannot tell adherence from failure.
Most people improve substantially. A meaningful minority do not fully recover. Nobody recovers quickly. Those three statements are what you can honestly promise.

Months, not weeks — and often more than a year. The conventional "one to three years" is widely quoted but rests on weak evidence, and as the natural history section sets out, the confident claim of complete spontaneous resolution has never been demonstrated.

What the better data suggest:

rows: 89% had normal or near-normal painless function at 2 years with pain-limited exercise; 64% within 12 months
Untreated patients regained some but not full range at 1–4 years
41% still symptomatic at a mean of 4.4 years

content.body: The spread between those figures is itself the honest answer: outcomes vary widely and we cannot predict an individual's.

Some permanent restriction is common, particularly in external rotation — and most patients function well despite it. The gap between measurably restricted and actually limited is wide in this condition, and worth naming for a patient who is fixated on the last 15 degrees.

• Recurrence in the same shoulder is uncommon. This is genuinely reassuring and worth saying
  • A substantial minority develop it in the opposite shoulder, usually at a different time. Tell them, so that if it happens they recognise it early rather than losing months
  • Simultaneous bilateral frozen shoulder is unusual — if you see it, reconsider the diagnosis (polymyalgia rheumatica, inflammatory arthritis)

rows: The strongest. More resistant to all treatments, slower to settle, worse outcomes after manipulation and release
Narrows the window in which injection works best

content.body: Note what is not on that list: imaging findings. Nothing on an MRI predicts how this patient will do.

Avoid both errors. "It will get better on its own in a year or two" is a promise the evidence does not support and the patient will hold you to. "There's nothing we can do" is false — injection and exercise reliably improve pain and function.

The accurate version:

content.label: Say it this way
content.text: "This takes many months, and I can't tell you exactly how many. What I can tell you is that the pain almost always settles before the stiffness does, that treatment makes that happen sooner and more comfortably, and that most people end up using the shoulder normally even if the last bit of rotation never quite comes back."

content.body:
Patients with frozen shoulder arrive in a particular state: in a lot of pain, often not sleeping, frequently told it is "just a frozen shoulder" in a tone that implied they should stop complaining. Many have been offered nothing.

Five messages.

content.text: 1 · Name it, and explain the mechanism simply

content.label: Say it this way
content.text: "The lining of your shoulder joint — the capsule — has become inflamed and then tightened up. It's not arthritis, nothing is torn, and the joint itself is fine. The capsule has shrunk, and that's why the arm won't go where you want it to."

content.body: Avoid "adhesive capsulitis" with patients. Nothing is stuck, and the word invites the idea of something that needs cutting free.
This is a genuinely painful condition, and saying so matters. The patient who has been told it is minor and will pass stops reporting how bad it is.

content.label: Say it this way
content.text: "This is one of the more painful shoulder problems there is, and the night pain is the part most people find hardest. We're going to treat that first."

content.label: Say it this way
content.text: "This takes months, not weeks. I can't tell you exactly how many, and anyone who gives you a precise figure is guessing. What I can tell you is the order: the pain settles before the stiffness does. You'll feel much better long before the arm moves properly again, and that's normal rather than a sign something is wrong."

content.body: Do not promise spontaneous full recovery in one to three years. The evidence does not support it, and they will remember.

content.text: 4 · The counterintuitive one — more stretching is not better

content.body: This is the message most likely to change the outcome, and the one patients find hardest to accept.

content.label: Say it this way
content.text: "Your instinct will be to force it, and to think that the harder you push the faster it'll free up. It's the opposite. Forcing an inflamed capsule makes it angrier and slower. You want to feel a stretch, not a pain — hold it gently for half a minute, and do that little and often through the day rather than one hard session."

content.body: The rule to give them:

content.label: Key Takeaway
content.text: A stretch, not a sharp pain. It should ease within a few minutes. And it must not wake you more that night. If it aches for an hour afterwards, that was too much — do less tomorrow, not more.

content.label: Say it this way
content.text: "Use it for everything it can still do. Protecting it completely is how this gets worse — and in some people, it's how it started."

content.body: Patients understand the plan better when the division of labour is explicit:

content.label: Say it this way
content.text: "The injection is for the pain. The exercises are for the movement. The injection won't loosen the shoulder, and the exercises won't settle the inflammation — that's why you need both, and why we do them in that order."

rows: Don't lie on that side. A small pillow under the elbow when on your back; hug a pillow when on the other side
"This is strongly linked to blood sugar, so we'll check it. And if you're diabetic, the steroid will push your sugars up for about a day — keep an eye on them"
"Some people get it on the other side later. If that happens, come early rather than waiting — the treatment works best in the first year"
Be specific about what is safe and what to adapt, rather than leaving them to guess
Pain not settling after the injection, no progress in range after a couple of months of consistent exercise, or anything new — particularly weakness

content.body:
Don't ask "does that make sense?" Ask:

  • "What are you going to tell people is wrong with your shoulder?" — tests message 1
  • "If the stretch is still aching an hour later, what do you do?" — tests message 4
  • "When do you think you'll be back to normal?" — tests message 3

If the answer to the second is "push through it", say it again differently. That belief will cost them months.

Diagnosis

  1. Loss of passive external rotation with the elbow at the side is the diagnosis. If passive range is preserved, look at the cuff instead.
  2. Active and passive range are restricted equally — the block is mechanical, not pain inhibition.
  3. The radiograph's job is to exclude osteoarthritis and locked posterior dislocation — the two conditions that produce the same finding. Get an axillary view.
  4. Do not interpret rotator cuff special tests in a stiff shoulder. They are all positive and all meaningless.
  5. Check HbA1c and thyroid function in everyone. Diabetes carries an odds ratio of about 3.7, and this may be the presentation that uncovers it.

Understanding it

6. Neither name is accurate. There are no adhesions; the capsule contracts. Use "frozen shoulder".

7. The classic self-limiting account is not supported. Untreated patients regain some but not full range, and most improvement happens early, not late.

8. Pain and stiffness are different problems — synovitis and neoinnervation versus capsular fibrosis — and they need different treatments.

Treatment

9. Offer intra-articular corticosteroid at first contact, especially within the first year. Combine it with a home exercise programme, always.

10. More stretching is not better. Pain-limited exercise outperformed intensive stretching (89% vs 63% near-normal at two years). Low load, long duration, little and often.

11. The injection treats the pain; the exercise treats the range. Neither substitutes for the other.

12. Escalate only after a genuine trial of injection plus exercise. UK FROST found manipulation and capsular release no better than structured physiotherapy at 12 months — and capsular release carried 4% serious adverse events against none for physiotherapy.

13. Manipulation is the most cost-effective escalation. Reserve arthroscopic release for selected refractory cases.

Prognosis

14. Months, not weeks. Pain settles before stiffness. Some residual restriction is common and usually not disabling.

15. Do not promise spontaneous resolution. Say what is true: treatment makes the course more comfortable and probably faster, and most people end up using the shoulder normally.
